title: Why did plague disappear from western Europe after the early eighteenth century?
short: After nearly four centuries of recurring epidemics, plague retreated from western and central Europe between the 1660s and the 1720s while persisting in the Ottoman Mediterranean, and no explanation commands agreement.
matters: The retreat of plague is one of the earliest large declines in European mortality, and its cause determines whether early modern states could control epidemic disease through quarantine, cordons and health passes, or whether the decline was ecological or biological and owed little to policy. The answer bears on demographic models of the eighteenth-century population rise, on the divergence between western Europe and the Ottoman and Russian lands where plague continued into the nineteenth century, and on current arguments about the efficacy of border controls against epidemics.
stuck: The retreat was gradual and uneven: London's last major epidemic was 1665, central Europe and the Baltic suffered in 1708–13, Provence in 1720–22, Messina in 1743, Moscow in 1771, and Noja (1815–16) and Mallorca (1820) saw late seaborne outbreaks, so any explanation must account for a moving frontier rather than a single date. Each main hypothesis (quarantine, rat or flea ecology, host immunity, climate, pathogen change) predicts the same broad outcome and is hard to falsify from mortality data alone. The genetic evidence has opened a parallel dispute over whether European plague was sustained by local reservoirs or repeatedly reintroduced from Asia, and ancient DNA samples remain few for the last outbreaks.
solved: A spatially explicit model, fitted to dated outbreak records and to the records of health offices on ship arrivals, quarantines and cordons, that reproduces the sequence and geography of the last western European outbreaks and correctly predicts which ports and regions escaped introduction when exposed, with its assumptions about reservoirs consistent with the ancient DNA phylogeny.
approach: Build a georeferenced, dated catalogue of plague outbreaks from 1650 to 1850 across Europe and the Mediterranean, starting from Biraben's inventory and extending it with regional studies, bills of mortality and parish registers, with source citations for every entry.

Extract arrivals, origins, bills of health, quarantine durations and lazaretto incidents from the health office archives of Marseille, Venice, Livorno, Genoa, Dubrovnik and Malta, which together record many near-misses where infected ships were stopped; much of this requires new digitization, building on the online Marseille captains' declarations of 1709–1852.

Link these to Levant shipping and consular reports of plague in Ottoman ports to estimate exposure for each European port by year, and test whether quarantine stringency, rather than exposure, explains which ports escaped.

Work with palaeogeneticists to sample burials from the last outbreaks (Provence, the Baltic, Messina, southern Italy, the Balkans) and with ecologists on rodent and flea faunal remains, so that reservoir and reintroduction scenarios can be tested against the documentary model.

existing.title: Les hommes et la peste en France et dans les pays européens et méditerranéens
existing.venue: 2 vols. Paris and The Hague: Mouton, 1975–1976
existing.note: Standard inventory of plague outbreaks in France and the Mediterranean to 1850, which credited sanitary cordons and maritime quarantine with the retreat.

existing.title: The Disappearance of Plague: A Continuing Puzzle
existing.note: Rejected the brown rat replacement theory on chronological grounds, doubted the efficacy of quarantine, and suggested instead that black rat populations acquired resistance.

existing.title: The Disappearance of Plague: An Alternative View
existing.note: Reply to Appleby arguing that human intervention, chiefly maritime quarantine and land cordons against reintroduction, was the decisive factor.

existing.title: Quarantaines et lazarets: l'Europe et la peste d'Orient (XVIIe–XXe siècles)
existing.note: History of the Mediterranean quarantine system that, with his work on plague in the Ottoman Empire, framed Europe's escape as protection against continuing Ottoman epidemics.

existing.title: The Retreat of Plague from Central Europe, 1640–1720: A Geomedical Approach
existing.venue: Bulletin of the History of Medicine 74 (1): 1–28
existing.note: Mapped the shrinking geography of outbreaks in central Europe and argued that plague contracted toward persistent regional foci rather than vanishing uniformly.

existing.title: Plague in seventeenth-century Europe and the decline of Italy: an epidemiological hypothesis
existing.note: Showed that the last seventeenth-century plagues struck southern Europe far harder than the north, a contrast that any account of the retreat must explain.

existing.authors: Boris V. Schmid, Ulf Büntgen, W. Ryan Easterday, Christian Ginzler, Lars Walløe, Barbara Bramanti and Nils Chr. Stenseth
existing.title: Climate-driven introduction of the Black Death and successive plague reintroductions into Europe
existing.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 112 (10): 3020–3025
existing.note: Linked European port outbreaks to tree-ring climate signals in Central Asia with a lag, arguing for repeated reintroductions from Asian rodent reservoirs rather than European foci.

existing.title: Plague and Empire in the Early Modern Mediterranean World: The Ottoman Experience, 1347–1600
existing.note: Reconstructed Ottoman plague chronology and argued for endemic foci within the empire, the source region against which western quarantine was directed.

existing.authors: Kirsten I. Bos, Alexander Herbig, Jason Sahl, Nicholas Waglechner, Mathieu Fourment, Stephen A. Forrest et al.
existing.title: Eighteenth century Yersinia pestis genomes reveal the long-term persistence of an historical plague focus
existing.note: Genomes from Marseille victims of 1722 descended from the Black Death lineage and matched no living focus, suggesting a now-extinct reservoir in or near Europe that persisted for centuries.

existing.authors: Katharine R. Dean, Fabienne Krauer, Lars Walløe, Ole Christian Lingjærde, Barbara Bramanti, Nils Chr. Stenseth and Boris V. Schmid
existing.title: Human ectoparasites and the spread of plague in Europe during the Second Pandemic
existing.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115 (6): 1304–1309
existing.note: Mortality models for nine outbreaks fit human flea and louse transmission better than rat-borne transmission, which bears on whether rat ecology could explain the retreat.

existing.authors: Maria A. Spyrou, Marcel Keller, Rezeda I. Tukhbatova, Christiana L. Scheib, Elizabeth A. Nelson, Aida Andrades Valtueña et al.
existing.title: Phylogeography of the second plague pandemic revealed through analysis of historical Yersinia pestis genomes
existing.note: Thirty-four genomes showed post-Black Death diversification into distinct clades that may have formed more than one reservoir in or near Europe, and a genomic deletion in late-pandemic strains.

existing.authors: Meriam Guellil, Oliver Kersten, Amine Namouchi, Stefania Luciani, Isolina Marota, Caroline A. Arcini et al.
existing.title: A genomic and historical synthesis of plague in 18th century Eurasia
existing.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 117 (45): 28328–28335
existing.note: Eighteenth-century genomes, including the first from the Caucasus, used to argue for introductions from reservoirs outside Europe during the pandemic's last phase.

existing.title: The Yellow Flag: Quarantine and the British Mediterranean World, 1780–1860
existing.note: Study of lazarettos and quarantine practice in Malta and the Mediterranean that assesses what the system did and did not achieve against plague.

existing.title: Perceptions of plague in eighteenth-century Europe
existing.note: Compared the last great epidemics in Germany, France and Moscow, showing unanimous official reliance on rigid quarantine amid deep medical division over contagion, and set western Europe against Ottoman and ancient DNA evidence.

existing.authors: Nils Chr. Stenseth, Yuxin Tao, Chutian Zhang, Barbara Bramanti, Ulf Büntgen et al.
existing.title: No evidence for persistent natural plague reservoirs in historical and modern Europe
existing.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 119 (51): e2209816119
existing.note: Argued from rodent and flea communities, soils and climate that western and central Europe could not sustain long-term wildlife reservoirs, supporting the reintroduction model against Bos et al.

archives.collection: Sous-série 200 E, Intendance sanitaire de Marseille (1640–1986), including captains' health declarations for arriving ships, 1709–1852
archives.note: Records of the Marseille health office, the main western gate for Levant trade; more than 100,000 images of ship declarations (origin, ports of call, cargo, health on board) are online.

archives.collection: Provveditori e sopraprovveditori alla sanità: deliberations, lazaretto records, bills of health, necrologi and reports from Venetian consuls in the Levant
archives.note: The oldest and most continuous health magistracy archive in Europe, recording intelligence on plague in Ottoman and Adriatic ports and the quarantine of ships and goods.

archives.repository: Državni arhiv u Dubrovniku (State Archives of Dubrovnik)
archives.collection: Records of the Ragusan health office and the Ploče lazaretto, on the overland caravan and maritime routes from the Ottoman Balkans
archives.note: Ragusa operated at the frontier with Ottoman plague and kept detailed health and quarantine records; access on site.

archives.repository: Chambre de commerce et d'industrie Aix-Marseille-Provence, archives and heritage collections
archives.collection: Correspondence of French consuls in the Levant and Barbary and Levant trade records
archives.note: Consular reports of plague in Ottoman ports, the source Panzac used to build the eastern Mediterranean chronology against which European exposure can be measured.

archives.collection: SP 105 (Levant Company records); PC 2 (Privy Council registers) with quarantine orders; customs and port records
archives.note: English Levant shipping and the orders imposing and lifting quarantine, including the response to Marseille in 1720–22.

archives.collection: Municipal records of the 1720–22 epidemic, including deliberations of the échevins and burial and hospital records
archives.note: The local record of the last major western European outbreak, needed to reconstruct its spread within the city and Provence.
